title: The AI Bill Is Too Damn High: Tokenomics 101 — Eugene Cheah, Featherless AI
talk_summary: Eugene Cheah of Featherless AI lays out a four-step tokenomics process — measure spend per key/team/use case, right-size models to workload, buy capacity matching tokens-per-second needs, and audit the human processes around AI. The core transferable ideas are splitting agentic (long-context, cache-heavy) from process (short, volume) workloads, using a smart-planner/cheap-worker split, and not paying for speed on background jobs.

takeaways.what_they_do: Use the strongest frontier model for planning and review, and a fast cheap model for the token-heavy implementation loop, since implementation is repetitive and a mid-tier model matches quality when the plan is good.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the planning and review agent is the best frontier close muscle model, and then the workers that implement it is the GRM 5.3 flash
takeaways.numbers: 5 devs, 8 agents, 116B tokens/mo on Opus ~$150k/mo → single node <$10k/mo with no disruption

takeaways.technique: Speed-tier by whether a human is waiting
takeaways.what_they_do: Pay for high tokens/sec only for interactive/human-facing work; run background/CI/agent jobs at low speed where throughput per GPU is far higher and cost per token drops.
takeaways.evidence_quote: background jobs, please don't run it at 120 tokens per second. It makes no sense
takeaways.numbers: 112 tok/s single request vs 16 parallel at ~half speed = ~10x total output, ~9-10x lower cost

takeaways.what_they_do: Split API keys by department/team/use case so token spend is attributable, then use that to right-size and to spot unproductive spend.
takeaways.evidence_quote: 30 40% of our customers that reach out to us, the first thing they had was a single shared key

takeaways.what_they_do: Expose models to users/agents as capability labels (fast, smart, finance-agent) rather than vendor names, so the underlying model can be swapped or A/B tested without changing prompts or workflows.
takeaways.evidence_quote: give department models labels, but not the model names

takeaways.technique: Cap change size to protect review throughput
takeaways.what_they_do: Large agent-generated changes overwhelm human/LLM reviewers, who then discard and re-implement; enforce smaller, modular changes and stronger automated tests so review isn't the bottleneck.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the bottleneck becomes the on the reviewer to merge the code ... they literally discard the first agent's job

takeaways.technique: Limit auto-routing to 2-3 models for cache hits
takeaways.what_they_do: Turn-level auto-routing across many models destroys prompt-cache hit rates; keep routing to at most two or three models, and prefer task/role-based routing over per-turn routing.
